question:
How to get the list of dates or global min/max timestamp from an openEO DataCube without downloading all data?

I'm working with openEO Python client and a multi-temporal satellite DataCube. I want to extract either: The list of all timestamps in the cube, or The global minimum and maximum dates across the temporal dimension. So far, I've tried: min_cube = cube.min_time() max_cube = cube.max_time() But these only collapse the temporal dimension and return a DataCube, not the actual dates. Moreover, when I visualize the results, it seems min and max might not correspond to chronological min/max: for example, in 2025 it shows more vegetation in the “min” result than in the “max”, when in Northern Hemisphere min should be in the winter and max for today (Oct2 2025) should be in September. I also checked: cube.metadata.extent["temporal"] But it returns something like ['2015-07-04T00:00:00Z', None] — just the declared collection bounds, not the actual dates present. What I want: A way to get all timestamps in the cube, or at least the earliest/latest date, without downloading all the raster data. Environment: Python 3.x openEO Python client 0.29+ Backend: openeo.dataspace.copernicus.eu/ Question: How can I get the actual list of time steps or global min/max timestamp from an openEO DataCube without downloading the full dataset? max image min image
reference_answer: The key point is that load_collection() in OpenEO doesn’t actually load or download data — it only builds a process graph (a declarative recipe of what should be computed later). The real data is only fetched when you call .execute() or .save_result(). So, if you want to get the list of timestamps (or min/max date) without downloading the whole raster, you can: Load just one lightweight band (e.g. "SCL" — Sentinel-2 Scene Classification Layer). Aggregate the data spatially so that you end up with one mean value per timestamp. Then call .execute() — it will return a small dictionary with timestamps as keys. Example # Example: Get timestamps for scenes in 2025 # with less than 10% cloud coverage in a given area year = "2025" cloud_cube = eoconn.load_collection( "SENTINEL2_L2A", temporal_extent=year, spatial_extent=dict(zip(["west", "north", "east", "south"], georectangle)), bands="SCL", max_cloud_cover=10, ) # Define SCL codes that correspond to clouds or shadows CLOUD_CODES = [3, 8, 9, 10, 11] # shadow, clouds, cirrus, etc. def is_cloud(data): is_cloud_mask = constant(0) for code in CLOUD_CODES: is_cloud_mask = is_cloud_mask.or_(data.eq(code)) return is_cloud_mask.int() # Spatial aggregation: mean cloud fraction per timestamp cloud_agg = ( cloud_cube .apply(is_cloud) .aggregate_spatial(geometries=polygon, reducer="mean") ) # Execute the process graph cloud_dict = cloud_agg.execute() print(cloud_dict) Example result { '2025-02-05T00:00:00Z': [[0.0]], '2025-02-10T00:00:00Z': [[0.0]], '2025-02-20T00:00:00Z': [[0.0]], '2025-03-19T00:00:00Z': [[0.0]], '2025-04-03T00:00:00Z': [[0.
llm_attempt:
cube.min_time()/max_time() reduce the temporal dimension per pixel/band using a min/max reducer on values, not on dates — each output pixel can come from a different timestamp, and different bands can effectively mix different acquisition dates. That's why the 'min' composite can look greener than 'max': it's not tied to any single date.

To get actual timestamps without downloading rasters: 1) Use the openEO process dimension_labels(cube, dimension='t') — in the Python client, cube.dimension_labels('t') — which returns just the temporal axis labels, not pixel data (still a tiny backend request, but no raster download). 2) Better, bypass the DataCube entirely and query the backend's STAC catalog directly with pystac-client (e.g. against the Copernicus Data Space STAC endpoint) using your bbox/collection/date filter — this returns exact item datetimes, is metadata-only, and is much cheaper than any openEO job. cube.metadata.extent only reflects the collection's declared bounds, not what's actually available for your filtered area, so it will never give you real per-scene dates.

question:
python customtkinter library - how to install

I need to install the customtkinter package for python. I used the command pip install customtkinter to install the package. When running pip list I can see the customtkinter package version. In the pycharm editor the package seam to get imported: Traceback (most recent call last): File "C:\Users\tal.d\PycharmProjects\py1.py\venv\1.py", line 1, in <module> import customtkinter ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'customtkinter' What am I doing wrong?
reference_answer: I would strongly recommend that you ensure that you are using a virtual environment (Virtualenv). You will get the option when you create a new project in Pycharm. You should also at this point be able to select a base Python interpreter. Click Create and then let Pycharm do its thing. Next go to File -> Settings and expand the link to your project name (just below Version Control). Now click Python Interpreter and you will see a display which includes the installed modules (you should see pip listed and a couple of others). Above the list of modules is a + icon. Click that and a popup will appear. Enter customtkinter into the search field at the top. You should see the module listed. Select it with your mouse and then click the Install Package at the bottom of the dialog. Keep an eye out for any errors. Once the package is installed you should be good to go. You can also check the venv directory, which sits in your project folder. If you drill down from there "venv > lib > PythonX.YY > site-packages", you should see a customtkinter folder. I think that on Windows, the PythonX.YY is not included in the path, so that would be something like: "venv > lib > site-packages" Oh and as suggested in another reply, I would avoid Anaconda. It seems there might be some issues there, when it comes to CustomTkinter.
llm_attempt: This is almost always an interpreter mismatch: pip install customtkinter installed the package into a different Python environment than the one PyCharm/your script is actually running. Your traceback shows the script executing from inside a virtual environment folder — check that: 1) that venv is activated in the terminal where you ran pip (prompt should show (venv)), 2) PyCharm's project interpreter (File > Settings > Project > Python Interpreter) is set to that same venv's python.exe, not the system Python or a different venv. Run pip list from inside the exact interpreter PyCharm uses to confirm they match. Safest fix: with the venv activated, run python -m pip install customtkinter (using python -m pip rather than a possibly-different pip on PATH), then restart PyCharm/the run configuration. If you have multiple Python installs, where python and where pip on Windows will often show they resolve to different locations, which is the classic cause of pip list showing a package while import still fails in the IDE.

question:
Python enum.Flag : best practice for creating "empty" and "full" flags

What is the "best" (as in, most likely to be intended and least likely to be deprecated/removed) way to create empty and full flags from enum.Flag ? Given the code: from __future__ import annotations import enum class Color(enum.Flag, boundary=enum.STRICT): RED = enum.auto() GREEN = enum.auto() BLUE = enum.auto() @staticmethod def black() -> Color: return Color(0) @staticmethod def white() -> Color: return Color(-1) print(Color.black()) # Color(0) print(Color.white()) # Color.RED|GREEN|BLUE Are Color(0) and Color(-1) the best way to create an empty/full flag respectively? The documentation does explicitly use the Color(0) idiom, thrice, in fact. Twice[ 1 ][ 2 ] in notices about changing "The repr() of zero-valued flags", and once[ 3 ] in an example for the __bool__ operator. I'm relatively comfortable about using this in production code, although I'd appreciate a more explicit "blessing" from the documentation for this idiom. Nevertheless, the Color(-1) is something I believe I haven't seen anywhere. As evidenced by the code, it works correctly even when the enum class has a STRICT boundary defined in its initialization. Is this "safe" for production usage? How much at risk is this of being deprecated/removed? Here are a few alternatives I've come up with: functools.reduce(operator.and_, Color) , for black , analogously with operator.or_ for white . I believe these maximize for "library intention", since it only uses explicitly defined operations between the elements ( __iter__ , __and__ , and __or__ .) ~Color.black() for white , or vice-versa, if it ends up that one idiom
reference_answer: The documentation for enum.Flag says specifically its members support the bitwise operators & ( AND ), | ( OR ), ^ ( XOR ), and ~ ( INVERT ); the results of those operations are (aliases of) members of the enumeration. so anything that uses the bitwise operators is using the documented interface and should be future-proof. One option is to choose a member, and xor it with itself, which produces an empty set. Then the inverse of the empty set is the full set. @classmethod def black(cls) -> typing.Self: return cls.RED ^ cls.RED @classmethod def white(cls) -> typing.Self: return ~cls.black() Another option, which doesn't require knowing member names, is to iterate the class to get all of the enum values, and or them together. That produces the full set, and the inverse of that is the empty set. (This is hypothetically slower than picking a single member, but it works on any enum.Flag class, and the time difference is unlikely to matter in practice.) @classmethod def white(cls) -> typing.Self: return functools.reduce(operator.__or__, cls) @classmethod def black(cls) -> typing.Self: return ~cls.white() In both cases you can wrap this with a trivial wrapper if __name__ == "__main__": print(repr(Color.black())) print(repr(Color.white())) which prints <Color: 0> <Color.RED|GREEN|BLUE: 7>
llm_attempt:
Color(0) is the documented, safe idiom for the empty flag — it's explicitly used in the stdlib docs and works fine under STRICT boundary since 0 trivially satisfies any boundary rule.

For 'full', prefer ~Color(0) over Color(-1). Flag's __invert__ (since the 3.11 Flag rewrite) is defined in terms of the class's own known members — it computes the complement within the defined bits, i.e. invert(empty) == all-members-set — rather than relying on raw two's-complement integer semantics. Color(-1) happens to work today because of how STRICT boundary canonicalizes negative values against the mask of defined bits, but that's an implementation detail of value coercion, not a documented contract, so it's more exposed to change across versions. ~Color(0) only uses operations (invert applied to a canonical empty member) that are explicitly part of Flag's public behavior. functools.reduce(operator.or_, Color) also works for 'full' and is fully explicit, but is more verbose with no real benefit over ~Color(0).

All .blk files processed.") if __name__ == "__main__": folder = r"C:\Users\user\Documents\First_folder\Second_folder" WordSwap(folder) The Python script itself is in First_folder and I use Spyder to run it. EDIT: I did enable full access via Properties -> Security. I then also tr
reference_answer: It seems likely that you do not have permission to modify some or all of the .blk files. This could be a matter of file level permissions or (because this is Windows rather than a proper operating system) it may be because the file is in use elsewhere. You could consider structuring your code to use an exception handler so that your entire program doesn't fail whenever there's such a problem. For example: from pathlib import Path SOURCE_DIR = Path("C:\\Users\\user\\Documents\\First_folder\\Second_folder") def word_swap(folder: Path) -> None: if folder.is_dir(): for file in folder.glob("*.blk"): try: with file.open() as blk: content = blk.read() new_content = content.replace("WORD", "NEWWORD") if content != new_content: backup = folder / (file.name + ".bak") file.replace(backup) with file.open("w") as blk: blk.write(new_content) except Exception as e: print(f"Error while processing {file.name} - {e}") else: print(f"Error: '{folder.name}' is not a valid directory.") if __name__ == "__main__": word_swap(SOURCE_DIR)
llm_attempt:
Full NTFS access in the Properties > Security tab doesn't rule out the other common causes of WinError 13 on Windows:

1) Another process has the file open/locked — most likely candidate given the folder structure (looks like a game's data files): the game/editor that owns these .blk files, or an antivirus real-time scan, can hold a lock that only shows up as permission denied from Python's side.
2) The file's own Read-only attribute (not the folder's) — right-click the specific .blk file > Properties > General tab > uncheck Read-only (separate from the Security/ACL tab you already checked).
3) If First_folder/Second_folder is inside OneDrive/Dropbox/Google Drive, background sync can transiently lock a file right as you try to write it.
4) Try running Spyder as Administrator once, to isolate whether it's a privilege issue vs a lock issue.

Also wrap the write in a short retry/backoff, since transient AV/sync locks often clear within a second.

question:
Multiclass focal loss in xgboost doesn't train

I have a dataframe with 60 columns as variables and a last column as target class (4 possible classes). I want to implement a custom loss function. I want that function to be the focal loss for a multiclass problem since I have a very imbalanced dataset. This is my approach following the docs from xgboost for custom functions: import numpy as np import xgboost from scipy.special import log_softmax, softmax from sklearn.utils import compute_sample_weight from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split num_classes = 4 def focal_loss_multiclass_objective(inputs: np.ndarray, dtrain: xgboost.DMatrix, alpha=1, gamma=2, num_classes=4): # Convert logits to probabilities and log-probabilities log_prob = log_softmax(inputs) prob = np.exp(log_prob) print(f"prob: {prob}") # One hot encoding the correct class targets = dtrain.get_label().astype(np.int64) targets_one_hot = np.identity(num_classes)[targets] # Gradient grad = -alpha*targets_one_hot*((1-prob)**(gamma-1)) * (-gamma*log_prob + (1-prob)/(prob+1e-6)) print(f"grad: {grad}") # Hessian hess = -alpha*targets_one_hot*(gamma*(gamma-1)*((1-prob)**(gamma-2)) * log_prob - 2*gamma*((1-prob)**(gamma-1))/(prob+1e-6) - ((1-prob)**gamma)/(prob+1e-6)**2) print("hess: ", hess) return grad, hess The gradient and hessian of the multiclass focal loss are kind of a hell, but I have double checked them with sympy. The training: X = df.iloc[:, 0:60] y = df.iloc[:, -1] X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42) # Sample weights: sample_weights = compute_sample_weight('balanced', y_train) print(np.un
reference_answer: xgboost passes the margins to your objective as a flat vector of length** n_samples × n_classes ** and expects you to return the gradient and Hessian in exactly the same 1-D shape. In the code above you return a 2-D array and you set the gradient of the “wrong” classes to zero, so three quarters of the positions that the booster is trying to update are always zero. With no usable gradient the model can only learn the prior - it stays at 0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25. A minimal focal-loss objective that works: def focal_multiclass(preds: np.ndarray, dtrain: xgb.DMatrix, num_class=4, gamma=2.0, alpha=0.25): # 1. reshape flat vector -> (N, C) preds = preds.reshape(-1, num_class) prob = softmax(preds, axis=1) y = dtrain.get_label().astype(int) onehot = np.eye(num_class)[y] # 2. p_t – probability of the true class pt = (onehot * prob).sum(1, keepdims=True) # 3. gradient for *all* classes grad = (alpha * (1 - pt) ** gamma) * (prob - onehot) # 4. a positive-definite Hessian (exact or a safe approximation) hess = (alpha * (1 - pt) ** gamma * (1 + gamma * pt * ( -np.log(np.clip(pt, 1e-7, 1)) ))) * prob * (1 - prob) # 5. flatten back return grad.ravel(), hess.ravel() Train: params = {"num_class": 4, "eval_metric": "mlogloss"} bst = xgb.train(params, dtrain, num_boost_round=200, obj=lambda p,d: focal_multiclass(p, d, num_class=4))
llm_attempt:
Two likely causes. First, shape/ordering: xgboost's custom multiclass objective expects grad and hess flattened in row-major (sample-major) order matching how it internally stores multi-class predictions — if you return a 2D (n_samples, num_classes) array where xgboost expects a flattened 1D array (or vice-versa depending on your xgboost version/API — native Booster vs sklearn, and whether multi_strategy='multi_output_tree' is set), the optimizer silently trains on garbage and looks like it doesn't train at all. Always flatten grad/hess consistently with how predt is shaped when it's passed in.

Second, and more likely given a hand-derived focal-loss Hessian: xgboost requires hess >= 0 per row for tree building to make sense, and it clips/handles non-positive Hessians in ways that can stall learning; a sign error in a manually-derived multiclass focal-loss Hessian (very easy to get wrong) commonly produces negative values. Validate grad/hess against autograd (torch.autograd) or finite differences before trusting the closed-form derivative, and print min/max of hess each round to check positivity.

question:
Python 3.13.5 sqlite3 DeprecationWarning persists despite registering custom date adapter

I am building an application using Python 3.13.5 and the native sqlite3 library. To correctly handle datetime.date objects and avoid the new DeprecationWarning , I am trying to implement the officially recommended custom adapter and converter pattern. Despite registering a custom adapter for the datetime.date type, the DeprecationWarning: The default date adapter is deprecated... is still being triggered every time I execute an INSERT statement with a date object. Interestingly, my custom converter (for reading DATE columns from the DB) seems to work correctly when I use the detect_types=sqlite3.PARSE_DECLTYPES flag. The problem seems to be exclusively with the adapter (for writing Python date objects to the DB), which appears to be ignored, causing sqlite3 to fall back to its deprecated default method. I have isolated the problem in the following minimal, self-contained script. This script does not use pytest or any external libraries. import sqlite3 from datetime import datetime, date import sys ############################################################################### print('\n') print(f'=' * 25, '--- PYTHON AND SQLITE3 VERSION ---', '=' * 25) print(f'Python Version: {sys.version}') print(f'Sqlite3 Version: {sqlite3.sqlite_version_info}') print(f'=' * 50) ############################################################################### #################### --- ADAPTERS AND CONVERSORS --- #################### def date_adapter(object_date: date) -> str: 'receives an object_date in the date adapter for adaptation to the new pattern of sqlite3' adapter_format_str = object
reference_answer: There's a subtle minor issue with date types. The import creates a datetime and a date objects but the registration uses datetime.date sqlite3.register_adapter(datetime.date, date_adapter) Using just date makes the warning go away and the adapter is called sqlite3.register_adapter(date, date_adapter) Add a print statement to verify def date_adapter(object_date: date) -> str: 'receives an object_date in the date adapter for adaptation to the new pattern of sqlite3' print('Adapter called') adapter_format_str = object_date.isoformat() return adapter_format_str Stdout: ========================= --- PYTHON AND SQLITE3 VERSION --- ========================= Python Version: 3.12.11 (main, Jun 10 2025, 09:17:07) [GCC] Sqlite3 Version: (3, 50, 2) ================================================== ========================= --- TYPE INPUT --- ========================= [DEBUG] Type Object Input in Database: <class 'datetime.date'> ================================================== ######################### --- WARNING HERE --- ######################### Adapter called ######################### --- WARNING HERE --- ######################### ========================= --- TYPE OUTPUT --- ========================= [DEBUG] Type Object Output from Database: <class 'str'> ================================================== As @j-earls pointed out in a comment datetime.date is a method >>> from datetime import datetime, date >>> datetime.date <method 'date' of 'datetime.datetime' objects> >>> date <class 'datetime.date'>
llm_attempt: Most likely cause: sqlite3's adapter registry keys on the exact type via type(obj), not via isinstance — so register_adapter(date, date_adapter) only fires when you insert an object whose exact type is datetime.date. Since datetime.datetime is a subclass of date, inserting a datetime instance (e.g. from datetime.now()) instead of a plain date won't match your registered adapter, and sqlite3 silently falls back to its deprecated built-in converter, triggering the warning. Check exactly what type you're passing into the INSERT — if it's ever a datetime rather than a date, you need a second explicit registration: sqlite3.register_adapter(datetime, datetime_adapter). Also double check you registered the adapter before opening/using the connection that performs the INSERT (registration is global but must happen before first use), and that you're not accidentally going through a second sqlite3.connect() call somewhere else that runs before your adapter registration executes. If both types are covered and it still warns, print type() of the value right before the INSERT to confirm what's actually being adapted.

llm_attempt:
query()'s 16384 cap is a hard per-request limit, so for ~3M rows you need to paginate rather than pull it all at once. The purpose-built tool for this is Milvus's QueryIterator (pymilvus): collection.query_iterator(batch_size=1000, expr='', output_fields=[...]), then repeatedly call .next() until it returns an empty list. It's designed exactly for full-collection export/scroll and works fine with a string primary key since it paginates internally using the PK as a cursor rather than requiring you to construct numeric ranges yourself.

For a full collection migration (not just export), consider milvus-backup (the official Milvus backup/restore tool) instead of query+insert — it exports a collection's data and schema and can restore/import it into a new collection, which is more robust and much faster than manually iterating 3M records and re-inserting them, and avoids hand-rolling pagination, retries, and dynamic-field schema mapping yourself.

question:
How to handle aiokafka getmany() exceptions in case of stopped kafka

I am runnging aiokafka consumer in fastAPI app In the main file I am starting the consumer from aiokafka import AIOKafkaConsumer def create_application() -> FastAPI: ... return FastAPI() app = create_application() consumer = create_consumer() @app.on_event("startup") async def startup_event(): """Start up event for FastAPI application.""" global_items["logger"].info("Starting up...") await consumer.start() asyncio.gather( consume(), # some other tasks return_exceptions=True ) async def consume(db: Session = next(get_db())): """Consume and process messages from Kafka.""" while True: try: print("Try consume") data = await consumer.getmany(timeout_ms=10000) for tp, msgs in data.items(): if msgs: for msg in msgs: await process_message(msg, db) await consumer.commit({tp: msgs[-1].offset+1}) except Exception as e: # printing ERROR LOG finally: await asyncio.sleep(settings.common.consumer_pause_sec) I want to print ERROR if kafka was stopped My actions Turn on Kafka and fastAPI application - see valid logs Trun off Kafka (via docker stop Current result after the actions - I see logs "Try consume" Expected result - I want to see Error log (in the exception handler)
reference_answer: This seems like it would be more of an asynchrony problem and not necessarily related to Kafka itself. When you issue your asyncio.gather(...) call, it isn't actually being awaited and likely won't handle any exceptions that would otherwise bubble up within its associated tasks as expected. You can consider introducing the await for that specific call which should create the necessary association within all of your tasks running within the gather() call and bubble up any exceptions that occur: async def startup_event(): logger.info("Starting up...") await consumer.start() try: await asyncio.gather( consume(), # Add your other tasks here ... ) except Exception as e: # Your logging output here finally: await consumer.stop() You can also consider using the return_exceptions option as well (which treats exceptions as results that you can handle accordingly): await asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True) The related docs provide a few different options and alternatives for handling this type of flow as well.
llm_attempt:
getmany() with a timeout just returns an empty dict when nothing arrives in that window — it does not raise when the broker itself is down. aiokafka's underlying client handles broker disconnects by retrying/reconnecting internally and logs that via its own logger (logging.getLogger('aiokafka')) rather than propagating an exception up through getmany(), which is why you only ever see 'Try consume' with no error hitting your except block — by design, transient broker outages are meant to be transparent/self-healing, not raised to caller code.

To actually detect/log a down broker: 1) configure logging so aiokafka's internal WARNING/ERROR logs (connection failures, metadata refresh failures) are visible in your app's output — that's the real signal Kafka is unreachable. 2) Add an explicit health check, e.g. periodically inspect consumer._client.ready(...) or the coordinator's connection state, or wrap consumer.start()/commit() (which can raise KafkaConnectionError/RequestTimedOutError) rather than expecting getmany() itself to surface the failure.

question:
Get bounding box of all the articles in a newspaper PDF file

I am trying to get the bounding box of all the articles in a newspaper pdf page using pdfplumber. However it is not marking all the articles. I am using the code below. import pdfplumber pdf = pdfplumber.open("2.pdf") p0 = pdf.pages[0] im = p0.to_image(resolution=150) table_settings = { "snap_y_tolerance": 0, "intersection_x_tolerance": 50, } im.debug_tablefinder(table_settings) tables = p0.find_tables(table_settings) im.show() Link to processed Image However, the it is not marking all articles as shown in image attached. I think the tables approach was the quickest and shortest way, but it works for well organised tables. I think this strategy is not suitable for newspaper articles. Any other suggestions or improvements in code will be appreciated.
llm_attempt:
find_tables()/table detection is the wrong primitive here — it looks for grid-like ruling lines or aligned text, which newspaper columns don't reliably have, so it will only ever catch layouts that coincidentally look tabular. For article segmentation you generally need two passes: (1) find column boundaries from large vertical whitespace gaps in page.extract_words() x-positions, (2) within each column, find article breaks from horizontal whitespace gaps between text blocks and/or headline detection using font size (extract_words(extra_attrs=['size','fontname']) — a jump to a larger/bolder font usually marks a new article's headline), then merge consecutive lines between headline breaks into one bounding box per article.

Hand-rolled gap/heuristic clustering with pdfplumber can work but is fragile on irregular newspaper grids. For something more robust, look at document layout analysis models purpose-built for this (LayoutParser with a PubLayNet-trained Detectron2/PaddleDetection model, or Docling), which segment multi-column print pages into article-level regions directly rather than relying on ruling lines.

question:
Use case of python decimal module VS float comparison

Recently I got to know the decimal python module. While I got to understand how to work with this, I still have a question that persists: What is/are the main case(s) where coders should use decimal.Decimal for float comparison? For example, at the past I have already performed some automatic tests for installable packages. At this ones, I always performed the comparison among floats with pytest.aprox() or by comparing the absolute difference with an epsilon value. Maybe my experience is still not enough to see which cases the decimal module is better. Could anyone provide some insights to me?
reference_answer: The main reasons to use decimal.Decimal over float type: 1. High-Precision decimal.Decimal is better chice if you want to get more accurate calculations, and to avoid rounding errors (because of Floating-point error mitigation ). 2. Exact Representation of Decimal Numbers Because of binary nature of float numbers, they sometimes cannot exactly represent many decimal numbers, for example: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 # False But when using decimal.Decimal : from decimal import Decimal Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2") == Decimal("0.3") # True 3. Using on different platforms float arithmetic operations results can be different across platform because different IEEE 754 implementation.
llm_attempt:
Decimal isn't really a better tool for float-vs-float comparison — the imprecision in an already-computed float comes from its binary representation, and Decimal can't retroactively fix that, so for testing numerical/scientific code your existing pytest.approx()/math.isclose()-with-epsilon approach is the right one and Decimal wouldn't help there.

Decimal's real use case is when the arithmetic itself must be done in exact base-10, not just compared afterward — money, invoicing, tax, accounting, anything with legally/contractually defined rounding rules. There you want 0.1 + 0.2 to equal exactly 0.30 and sums of currency amounts to never accumulate binary rounding drift in the first place, with explicit control over precision and rounding mode via decimal.getcontext(). So the dividing line isn't comparison strategy, it's domain: use Decimal when the underlying quantities are inherently decimal/discrete (currency, quantities with defined decimal places) and correctness of the arithmetic itself matters; use float plus tolerance comparison for continuous numerical/scientific computation where binary floating point is the natural representation.

So the final folder should have three images (the first image would contain 4 images, the second image would contain 4 images, the third image would contain 1 image)
reference_answer: Does this do what you're looking for? It uses more_itertools.chunked to get image file paths in groups of four, including the final group which may be less than four. I also rewrote your concatenation function to accept any number of images, and expand to fit the widest one, if their widths differ. from pathlib import Path from more_itertools import chunked from PIL import Image def concat_images(*images): """Generate composite of all supplied images.""" # Get the widest width. width = max(image.width for image in images) # Add up all the heights. height = sum(image.height for image in images) composite = Image.new('RGB', (width, height)) # Paste each image below the one before it. y = 0 for image in images: composite.paste(image, (0, y)) y += image.height return composite if __name__ == '__main__': # Define the folder to operate on (currently set to the current # working directory). images_dir = Path('.') # Define where to save the output (shown here, will be in `output` # inside the images dir). output_dir = images_dir / 'output' # Create the output folder, if it doesn't already exist. output_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True) # Iterate through the .png files in groups of four, using an index # to name the resulting output. png_paths = images_dir.glob('*.png') for i, paths in enumerate(chunked(png_paths, 4), start=1): images = [Image.open(path) for path in paths] composite = concat_images(*images) composite.save(output_dir / f'{i}.png')
llm_attempt:
Generalize get_concat_v to take a list, then chunk the folder's files into groups of 4:

import os
from PIL import Image

def concat_v(images):
    w = max(im.width for im in images)
    h = sum(im.height for im in images)
    dst = Image.new('RGB', (w, h), 'white')
    y = 0
    for im in images:
        dst.paste(im, (0, y))
        y += im.height
    return dst

folder, out = 'images', 'output'
os.makedirs(out, exist_ok=True)
files = sorted(f for f in os.listdir(folder) if f.lower().endswith(('.png', '.jpg', '.jpeg')))

for i in range(0, len(files), 4):
    chunk = files[i:i+4]
    imgs = [Image.open(os.path.join(folder, f)) for f in chunk]
    concat_v(imgs).save(os.path.join(out, f'concat_{i//4+1}.png'))

For 9 images this naturally yields 3 outputs (4, 4, then 1 leftover) since the last slice just has fewer items — concat_v works fine with a single image too. Sort filenames first so grouping is deterministic.

The mangled name (a tilde-prefixed leftover folder such as ~atplotlib) is a classic remnant of a previously interrupted pip uninstall/upgrade sitting in site-packages; removing it was correct. Requirement already satisfied now confirms matplotlib 3.10.7 is installed into your Anaconda base environment's site-packages — but if the Jupyter kernel you're actually running isn't that same Anaconda base interpreter (a different conda env, or a stale kernelspec pointing elsewhere), import will still fail there.

question:
Masked aggregations in pytorch

Given data and mask tensors are there a pytorch-way to obtain masked aggregations of data (mean, max, min, etc.)? x = torch.tensor([ [1, 2, -1, -1], [10, 20, 30, -1] ]) mask = torch.tensor([ [True, True, False, False], [True, True, True, False] ]) To compute a masked mean I can do the following, yet are there any pytorch built-in or commonly used package to do that? n_mask = torch.sum(mask, axis=1) x_mean = torch.sum(x * mask, axis=1) / n_mask print(x_mean) > tensor([ 1.50, 20.00])
reference_answer: If you don't want to use torch.masked due to it being in prototype stage, you can use scatter_reduce to aggregate based on sum, prod, mean, amax and amin. x = torch.tensor([ [1, 2, -1, -1], [10, 20, 30, -1] ]).float() # note you'll need to cast to float for this to work mask = torch.tensor([ [True, True, False, False], [True, True, True, False] ]) rows, cols = mask.nonzero().T for reduction in ['mean', 'sum', 'prod', 'amax', 'amin']: output = torch.zeros(x.shape[0], device=x.device, dtype=x.dtype) output = output.scatter_reduce(0, rows, x[rows, cols], reduce=reduction, include_self=False) print(f"{reduction}\t{output}") # # printed output: # mean tensor([ 1.5000, 20.0000]) # sum tensor([ 3., 60.]) # prod tensor([2.0000e+00, 6.0000e+03]) # amax tensor([ 2., 30.]) # amin tensor([ 1., 10.])
llm_attempt:
No single built-in covers all reductions, but the standard idioms:

Mean (what you have) is the canonical approach: (x*mask).sum(dim)/mask.sum(dim).

Max/min: fill masked-out entries with the reduction's identity element first, then use the ordinary reduction:
x.masked_fill(~mask, float('-inf')).max(dim=1)
x.masked_fill(~mask, float('inf')).min(dim=1)

PyTorch also has a prototype torch.masked (MaskedTensor) API meant to be the proper built-in answer:
mt = torch.masked.masked_tensor(x.float(), mask)
mt.mean(dim=1), mt.amax(dim=1), mt.amin(dim=1), mt.sum(dim=1)
This handles mean/amax/amin/sum consistently without manual identity-element juggling, but as of recent PyTorch releases it's still labeled prototype/beta, so API details can change between versions — fine for research code, worth pinning your torch version if you depend on it in production.

question:
How to find the indexes of the first $n$ maximum values of a tensor?

I know that torch.argmax(x, dim = 0) returns the index of the first maximum value in x along dimension 0 . But is there an efficient way to return the indexes of the first n maximum values? If there are duplicate values I also want the index of those among the n indexes. As a concrete example, say x=torch.tensor([2, 1, 4, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1]) . I would like a function generalized_argmax(xI torch.tensor, n: int) such that generalized_argmax(x, 4) returns [0, 2, 4, 5] in this example.
reference_answer: To acquire all you need you have to go over the whole tensor. The most efficient should therefore be to use argsort afterwards limited to n entries. >>> x=torch.tensor([2, 1, 4, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1]) >>> x.argsort(dim=0, descending=True)[:n] [2, 4, 0, 5] Sort it again to get [0, 2, 4, 5] if you need the ascending order of indices.
llm_attempt:
Use a stable descending argsort so ties keep their original (first-occurrence) index order, then take the first n:

def generalized_argmax(x, n):
    order = torch.argsort(x, descending=True, stable=True)
    return torch.sort(order[:n]).values

argsort's stable=True (PyTorch >= 1.9) guarantees equal values keep their relative input order rather than an arbitrary one, which is exactly what 'first n maximum values, including duplicates in order' needs. For x = [2,1,4,1,4,2,1,1], stable descending order is [2,4,0,5,1,3,6,7] (the two 4's by index, then the two 2's by index, then the 1's); taking the first 4 gives {2,4,0,5}, and sorting ascending gives [0,2,4,5] — matching your expected output.

torch.topk(x, n) returns n largest values/indices too, but its tie-breaking order isn't documented/guaranteed the way stable=True is, so prefer argsort(stable=True) if you need deterministic first-occurrence tie-breaking.

question:
How can I host a Jupyter Notebook (.ipynb)

How can I host a Jupyter Notebook (.ipynb) file online so others can easily access, view, and run it? I'm looking for simple platforms or methods that allow sharing notebooks publicly without requiring users to install anything locally.
reference_answer: Google Collab or CoCalc should work well, depending on your constraints.
llm_attempt:
A few standard options depending on whether you want viewable vs actually runnable:

Viewable only, zero setup: push it to a public GitHub repo — GitHub renders .ipynb files automatically in the browser. Or paste any URL to the notebook into nbviewer.org for a clean rendered view.

Actually runnable in-browser, no local install:
1) Google Colab — upload the notebook or open it from GitHub/Drive, then share the Colab link (set sharing to 'Anyone with the link'); viewers can run all cells for free.
2) Binder (mybinder.org) — point it at a public GitHub repo containing the notebook plus a requirements.txt/environment.yml; it builds a temporary live Jupyter environment and gives you a shareable link where anyone can execute cells with no install, good for reproducible environments.
3) Kaggle Notebooks or Deepnote are similar hosted/runnable alternatives.

Best combo for public sharing: a GitHub repo (viewing + version control) plus a Binder badge in the README (one-click execution).

question:
Private AI Chatbot

How to build an AI-powered chatbot for a company that can answer users' questions based on company-specific data, interact with users through natural question-and-answer conversations similar to other advanced chatbots (such as ChatGPT, Claude, or DeepSeek), calculate stock levels, and intelligently suggest whether to reorder products along with recommended reorder quantities?

llm_attempt:
This is really two systems combined, not one:

1) The Q&A-over-company-data part is a RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) pipeline: chunk and embed your internal documents into a vector database (Chroma, FAISS, pgvector, Pinecone), retrieve the most relevant chunks per user query, and pass them as context to an LLM to generate the answer. Use a framework like LangChain or LlamaIndex to wire this together. Private typically means either self-hosting an open model (Llama/Mistral via Ollama/vLLM) or using an enterprise API plan with no data retention/training on your data.

2) Stock levels and reorder suggestions are not something an LLM should compute from scratch — write that as ordinary business logic/SQL against your inventory database (e.g. reorder_qty = forecasted_demand_over_lead_time + safety_stock - current_stock), expose it as a function/tool, and let the chatbot call that tool via function-calling/agentic tool-use rather than asking the LLM to reason numbers directly.

This is a large build (weeks, not a snippet) — happy to go deeper on any one piece.

Those two error messages together suggest a routing/permissioning conflict rather than a simple field typo: PostToATS is only meaningful for orders routed to specific ATS destinations, and it looks like your account/order combination is being rejected both for including it and (per the second message) for the order type requiring it, depending on how IB's backend resolves routing for PEG BEST plus IBKRATS.
